title: Αἰνείου γενεή
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Aeneas answers that he will not be frightened by words like a child: each knows the other’s parentage by report. He is the son of Anchises and Aphrodite, Achilles of Peleus and Thetis, and one pair of parents will mourn today. He then recites his descent from Zeus through Dardanus, Erichthonius (whose three thousand mares the North Wind covered in the shape of a horse), Tros, Assaracus, Capys and Anchises, with Ganymede and Priam’s line branching off, and says that Zeus raises and lowers men’s excellence as he pleases. Quarrelling is for women, and he wants bronze. His spear pierces two of the five metal layers of Achilles’ shield and is stopped by the gold. Achilles’ spear tears through the circles of Aeneas’ shield and sticks in the ground behind him. As Achilles rushes in with his sword and Aeneas lifts a huge stone, Poseidon sees it and tells the watching gods that Aeneas, who is blameless, is doomed because he obeyed Apollo. They must save him, lest Zeus be angered and the line of Dardanus vanish: Zeus now hates Priam’s line, and the might of Aeneas and his children’s children will rule the Trojans.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Αἰνείας ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aut’ Aineias apameibeto phōnēsen te·
sentences.l: Him then in turn answered Aeneas, and spoke:
sentences.i: Then Aeneas answered him in turn, and spoke:
sentences.n: A reply-formula: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ … ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε ‘him then in turn answered … and spoke’. αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’, ἀπαμείβετο the imperfect of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’, φώνησεν the aorist of φωνέω ‘speak’. Αἰνείας is Aeneas, whom Apollo has sent against Achilles. The colon opens his reply to Achilles’ warning, and the paragraph break marks the change of speaker.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδη μὴ δὴ ἐπέεσσί με νηπύτιον ὣς
ἔλπεο δειδίξεσθαι, ἐπεὶ σάφα οἶδα καὶ αὐτὸς
ἠμὲν κερτομίας ἠδ’ αἴσυλα μυθήσασθαι.
sentences.tr:
Pēleïdē mē dē epeessi me nēpytion hōs
elpeo deidixesthai, epei sapha oida kai autos
ēmen kertomias ēd’ aisyla mythēsasthai.
sentences.l:
“Son of Peleus, do not indeed with words me, like a babe,
hope to frighten, since clearly I know, even myself,
both taunts and wicked things to speak.
sentences.i: “Son of Peleus, do not hope to frighten me with words as though I were a child, since I too know well how to speak both taunts and wicked things.
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδη is the vocative of the patronymic Πηλεΐδης ‘son of Peleus’, here Achilles. μὴ … ἔλπεο is a prohibition: ἔλπεο is the imperative of ἔλπομαι ‘hope, expect’, and δειδίξεσθαι is a future infinitive of δειδίσσομαι ‘frighten’. νηπύτιον ὣς ‘like a babe’ describes με. σάφα ‘clearly’; οἶδα ‘I know’. κερτομίας ‘taunts’ and αἴσυλα ‘wicked things’ are the objects of μυθήσασθαι ‘to speak’, joined by ἠμέν … ἠδ’ ‘both … and’.

sentences.t:
ἴδμεν δ’ ἀλλήλων γενεήν, ἴδμεν δὲ τοκῆας
πρόκλυτ’ ἀκούοντες ἔπεα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.tr:
idmen d’ allēlōn geneēn, idmen de tokēas
proklyt’ akouontes epea thnētōn anthrōpōn·
sentences.l:
And we know each other’s lineage, and we know the parents,
hearing far-famed words of mortal men;
sentences.i: We each know the other’s lineage and the other’s parents from hearing the far-famed words of mortal men;
sentences.n: ἴδμεν is the epic first plural of οἶδα ‘know’ (Attic ἴσμεν). ἀλλήλων ‘of each other’ goes with both γενεήν ‘lineage’ and τοκῆας ‘parents’. πρόκλυτα ‘far-famed’ agrees with ἔπεα (Attic ἔπη), the plural of ἔπος ‘word’. ἀκούοντες ‘hearing’ says how they know: by report, as the next line makes plain, since neither has met the other’s parents.

sentences.t: ὄψει δ’ οὔτ’ ἄρ πω σὺ ἐμοὺς ἴδες οὔτ’ ἄρ’ ἐγὼ σούς.
sentences.tr: opsei d’ out’ ar pō sy emous ides out’ ar’ egō sous.
sentences.l: but by sight neither then have you yet seen mine, nor I yours.
sentences.i: But you have not yet seen my parents with your eyes, nor have I seen yours.
sentences.n: ὄψει is the dative of ὄψις ‘sight’, ‘by sight’. ἐμούς ‘mine’ and σούς ‘yours’ are masculine plural and stand for ‘my parents’ and ‘your parents’ from the line before; the noun is left unsaid. οὔτ’ … οὔτ’ ‘neither … nor’. ἄρ and πω ‘yet’ are light particles. ἴδες is the aorist of ὁράω ‘see’; the second clause leaves out the verb.

sentences.t:
φασὶ σὲ μὲν Πηλῆος ἀμύμονος ἔκγονον εἶναι,
μητρὸς δ’ ἐκ Θέτιδος καλλιπλοκάμου ἁλοσύδνης·
sentences.tr:
phasi se men Pēlēos amymonos ekgonon einai,
mētros d’ ek Thetidos kalliplokamou halosydnēs·
sentences.l:
They say that you are of Peleus, the blameless, the offspring,
and of a mother, from Thetis, fair-plaited, Halosydne;
sentences.i: They say that you are the offspring of blameless Peleus, and that your mother is fair-plaited Thetis, Halosydne;
sentences.n: φασί ‘they say’ takes the accusative and infinitive: σὲ … ἔκγονον εἶναι ‘that you are the offspring’. Πηλῆος is the epic genitive of Πηλεύς, with ἀμύμονος ‘blameless’, a stock epithet whose exact sense is not certain; it is translated every time. μητρὸς … ἐκ Θέτιδος ‘from mother Thetis’. καλλιπλοκάμου ‘fair-plaited’ is καλλι- ‘fair’ with πλόκαμος ‘plait’. ἁλοσύδνης is a second name of Thetis, kept as a name because its meaning is not known.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν υἱὸς μεγαλήτορος Ἀγχίσαο
εὔχομαι ἐκγεγάμεν, μήτηρ δέ μοί ἐστ’ Ἀφροδίτη·
sentences.tr:
autar egōn huios megalētoros Anchisao
euchomai ekgegamen, mētēr de moi est’ Aphroditē·
sentences.l:
but I, as son of great-spirited Anchises,
claim to have been born, and my mother is Aphrodite;
sentences.i: But I claim to be the son of great-spirited Anchises, and my mother is Aphrodite;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ sets Aeneas against Achilles. ἐγών is ἐγώ with an added -ν. μεγαλήτορος ‘great-spirited’ is a stock epithet, translated the same each time; Ἀγχίσαο has the epic genitive -αο (Attic -ου). εὔχομαι with an infinitive is ‘I claim’; ἐκγεγάμεν is the perfect infinitive of ἐκγίγνομαι ‘be born of’ (Attic ἐκγεγονέναι). μοί ἐστ’ is ‘to me is’, that is, ‘my mother is’. Line 208 is metrically irregular as transmitted: Ἀγχίσαο fills the last two feet only if its short ι and its short -σα- are both counted long, which gives a spondee in the fifth foot.

sentences.t:
τῶν δὴ νῦν ἕτεροί γε φίλον παῖδα κλαύσονται
σήμερον·
sentences.tr:
tōn dē nyn heteroi ge philon paida klausontai
sēmeron·
sentences.l:
Of these, one pair or the other a dear son will weep for
today;
sentences.i: One pair of parents or the other will weep for a dear son today;
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of these’ is partitive with ἕτεροι ‘the one or the other’: Aeneas means that either his parents or Achilles’ will be in mourning before the day is out, and the English supplies ‘pair of parents’. κλαύσονται is the future middle of κλαίω and takes the accusative: ‘will weep for a dear son’ (παῖς ‘child, son’). σήμερον ‘today’ ends the sentence at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ φημ’ ἐπέεσσί γε νηπυτίοισιν
ὧδε διακρινθέντε μάχης ἐξαπονέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
ou gar phēm’ epeessi ge nēpytioisin
hōde diakrinthente machēs exaponeesthai.
sentences.l:
for I do not say that by babes’ words, at any rate,
thus parted, we two will come back out of the battle.
sentences.i: for I do not think the two of us will be parted like this, by a child’s talk, and come back out of the battle.
sentences.n: οὐ … φημί with an infinitive is ‘I do not say that … will’, so ‘I do not think’. ἐξαπονέεσθαι ‘come back out’ is a present infinitive with future sense. νηπυτίοισιν (from νηπύτιος ‘like a babe’) agrees with ἐπέεσσι, the epic dative plural of ἔπος ‘word’. διακρινθέντε is a dual aorist passive participle, ‘the two of us parted’; the dual is the Greek number for a pair. ὧδε ‘thus’; μάχης is a genitive of separation.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις καὶ ταῦτα δαήμεναι, ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῇς
ἡμετέρην γενεήν, πολλοὶ δέ μιν ἄνδρες ἴσασι·
sentences.tr:
ei d’ etheleis kai tauta daēmenai, ophr’ eÿ eidēis
hēmeterēn geneēn, polloi de min andres isasi·
sentences.l:
But if you wish also these things to learn, so that well you may know
our lineage — and many men know it —
sentences.i: But if you also wish to learn this, so that you may know our lineage well (and many men know it):
sentences.n: εἰ … ἐθέλεις … δαήμεναι is ‘if you wish to learn’ (δαήμεναι, the aorist infinitive of δάω). ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῇς is a purpose clause, ‘so that you may know well’, with the subjunctive of οἶδα; the diaeresis in ἐῢ is the edition’s. ἡμετέρην γενεήν ‘our lineage’ is the object, and ἴσασι is the third plural of οἶδα. Glaucus begins his own genealogy with the same words at 6.150, and the English is the same.

sentences.t:
Δάρδανον αὖ πρῶτον τέκετο νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς,
κτίσσε δὲ Δαρδανίην, ἐπεὶ οὔ πω Ἴλιος ἱρὴ
ἐν πεδίῳ πεπόλιστο πόλις μερόπων ἀνθρώπων,
ἀλλ’ ἔθ’ ὑπωρείας ᾤκεον πολυπίδακος Ἴδης.
sentences.tr:
Dardanon au prōton teketo nephelēgereta Zeus,
ktisse de Dardaniēn, epei ou pō Ilios hirē
en pediōi pepolisto polis meropōn anthrōpōn,
all’ eth’ hypōreias ōikeon polypidakos Idēs.
sentences.l:
Dardanus, in turn, first did cloud-gatherer Zeus beget,
and he founded Dardania, since not yet sacred Ilium
in the plain had been built, a city of speech-dividing men,
but they still dwelt in the foothills of many-springed Ida.
sentences.i: Zeus who gathers the clouds first begot Dardanus, and Dardanus founded Dardania, for sacred Ilium, a city of men of articulate speech, had not yet been built in the plain, and they still lived in the foothills of many-springed Ida.
sentences.n: Δάρδανον is the object and Ζεύς the subject, as the endings show; the first line of the literal English keeps the Greek order, so read it ‘Zeus first begot Dardanus’. νεφεληγερέτα ‘cloud-gatherer’ is Zeus’ stock epithet. κτίσσε is the unaugmented aorist of κτίζω ‘found’, and Dardanus is the founder. πεπόλιστο is the pluperfect passive of πολίζω ‘build as a city’. The meaning of μερόπων is not known; the ancient explanation ‘with divided speech’ is followed. ὑπωρείας ‘foothills’ is accusative; ᾤκεον ‘they were living’; πολυπίδακος ‘of many springs’.

sentences.t:
Δάρδανος αὖ τέκεθ’ υἱὸν Ἐριχθόνιον βασιλῆα,
ὃς δὴ ἀφνειότατος γένετο θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.tr:
Dardanos au teketh’ huion Erichthonion basilēa,
hos dē aphneiotatos geneto thnētōn anthrōpōn·
sentences.l:
Dardanus in turn begot a son, Erichthonius the king,
who indeed became the richest of mortal men;
sentences.i: Dardanus in turn begot a son, King Erichthonius, who became the richest of mortal men;
sentences.n: τέκεθ’ is τέκετο, elided, the aorist middle of τίκτω ‘beget’ (of a father; of a mother, ‘bear’). βασιλῆα is the epic accusative of βασιλεύς ‘king’, in apposition to Ἐριχθόνιον. ὃς δή … ‘who indeed’. ἀφνειότατος is the superlative of ἀφνειός ‘rich’, with the genitive θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων ‘of mortal men’. The same ‘most … of mortal men’ turns up for Ganymede at 233.

sentences.t:
τοῦ τρισχίλιαι ἵπποι ἕλος κάτα βουκολέοντο
θήλειαι, πώλοισιν ἀγαλλόμεναι ἀταλῇσι.
sentences.tr:
tou trischiliai hippoi helos kata boukoleonto
thēleiai, pōloisin agallomenai atalēisi.
sentences.l:
Of him three thousand horses along the marsh were pastured,
female, exulting in tender foals.
sentences.i: He had three thousand mares pastured along the marsh, exulting in their tender foals.
sentences.n: ἵπποι is feminine here, as τρισχίλιαι ‘three thousand’ and θήλειαι ‘female’ show: mares. τοῦ ‘of him’ is Erichthonius. ἕλος κάτα is κατὰ ἕλος, the preposition set after its noun, ‘down along the marsh’. βουκολέοντο is the passive of βουκολέω ‘tend, pasture’, so ‘were pastured’. ἀγαλλόμεναι ‘exulting’; ἀταλῇσι from ἀταλός ‘tender, frisky’ goes with πώλοισιν, the epic dative plural of πῶλος ‘foal’; ἀταλῇσι is feminine, so πώλοισιν is read as feminine here (young mares).

sentences.t:
τάων καὶ Βορέης ἠράσσατο βοσκομενάων,
ἵππῳ δ’ εἰσάμενος παρελέξατο κυανοχαίτῃ·
sentences.tr:
taōn kai Boreēs ērassato boskomenaōn,
hippōi d’ eisamenos parelexato kyanochaitēi·
sentences.l:
Of these, as they grazed, even the North Wind fell in love,
and, making himself like a horse, dark-haired, lay beside them;
sentences.i: Even the North Wind fell in love with them as they grazed, and, making himself like a dark-haired horse, lay beside them;
sentences.n: τάων is the epic genitive plural of the demonstrative, ‘of these’, with the participle βοσκομενάων ‘as they grazed’. ἠράσσατο, aorist of ἐράομαι ‘fall in love with’, takes the genitive. Βορέης is the North Wind. εἰσάμενος is the aorist participle of εἴδομαι, ‘making himself like’, with the dative ἵππῳ κυανοχαίτῃ ‘a dark-haired horse’ (κύανος ‘dark blue’, χαίτη ‘mane, hair’). παρελέξατο ‘lay beside’.

sentences.t: αἳ δ’ ὑποκυσάμεναι ἔτεκον δυοκαίδεκα πώλους.
sentences.tr: hai d’ hypokysamenai etekon dyokaideka pōlous.
sentences.l: and they, having conceived, bore twelve foals.
sentences.i: and they conceived and bore twelve foals.
sentences.n: αἳ is the demonstrative ‘they’, the mares. ὑποκυσάμεναι is the aorist participle of ὑποκύομαι ‘conceive’. ἔτεκον is the aorist of τίκτω, ‘bore’ because the mothers are the subject. δυοκαίδεκα is ‘twelve’ (δύο καὶ δέκα), πώλους ‘foals’.

sentences.t:
αἳ δ’ ὅτε μὲν σκιρτῷεν ἐπὶ ζείδωρον ἄρουραν,
ἄκρον ἐπ’ ἀνθερίκων καρπὸν θέον οὐδὲ κατέκλων·
sentences.tr:
hai d’ hote men skirtōien epi zeidōron arouran,
akron ep’ antherikōn karpon theon oude kateklōn·
sentences.l:
And they, whenever they bounded over the grain-giving plough-land,
ran on the tip of the fruit of the ears, and did not break it;
sentences.i: Whenever they bounded over the grain-giving plough-land, they ran along the very tops of the ears and did not break them;
sentences.n: σκιρτῷεν is the optative of σκιρτάω ‘bound, leap’, used of what happened again and again (‘whenever they bounded’); θέον ‘they ran’ is the imperfect of θέω. ζείδωρον ‘grain-giving’ comes from ζειά, a kind of grain; the ancients also took it as ‘life-giving’. ἄκρον ἐπ’ … ‘on the very top of’. ἀνθερίκων καρπόν is ‘the fruit of the ἀνθέρικες’; the meaning of ἀνθερίκων is not certain: ‘ears of grain’ is followed (so ‘the ears’ in the English), ‘asphodel stalks’ is the other guess. κατέκλων is the imperfect of κατακλάω ‘break down’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ σκιρτῷεν ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης,
ἄκρον ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνος ἁλὸς πολιοῖο θέεσκον.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē skirtōien ep’ eurea nōta thalassēs,
akron epi rhēgminos halos polioio theeskon.
sentences.l:
But whenever they bounded over the broad back of the sea,
at the top of the surf-line of the grey sea they would run.
sentences.i: but whenever they bounded over the sea’s broad back, they would run along the tops of the breaking surf of the grey sea.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή … takes up the clause before: ‘but whenever’. εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης ‘the broad back of the sea’ is the open sea. ῥηγμῖνος is the genitive of ῥηγμίν ‘the place where the sea breaks’; here the mares run on the breaking waves, so the English has ‘surf’. ἁλὸς πολιοῖο ‘of the grey sea’. θέεσκον is a frequentative imperfect in -εσκον, ‘they would run’.

sentences.t: Τρῶα δ’ Ἐριχθόνιος τέκετο Τρώεσσιν ἄνακτα·
sentences.tr: Trōa d’ Erichthonios teketo Trōessin anakta·
sentences.l: and Tros Erichthonius begot, a lord for the Trojans;
sentences.i: Erichthonius begot Tros, a lord for the Trojans;
sentences.n: Τρῶα is the accusative of Τρώς, Tros, the ancestor from whom the Trojans take their name, and Ἐριχθόνιος is the subject of τέκετο ‘begot’. ἄνακτα ‘lord’ is in apposition to Τρῶα, and the dative Τρώεσσιν ‘for the Trojans’ is the epic form in -εσσιν.

sentences.t:
Τρωὸς δ’ αὖ τρεῖς παῖδες ἀμύμονες ἐξεγένοντο
Ἶλός τ’ Ἀσσάρακός τε καὶ ἀντίθεος Γανυμήδης,
ὃς δὴ κάλλιστος γένετο θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.tr:
Trōos d’ au treis paides amymones exegenonto
Ilos t’ Assarakos te kai antitheos Ganymēdēs,
hos dē kallistos geneto thnētōn anthrōpōn·
sentences.i: and to Tros in turn three blameless sons were born, Ilus and Assaracus and godlike Ganymede, who became the most beautiful of mortal men;
sentences.n: Τρωὸς is the genitive of Τρώς. ἐξεγένοντο is the aorist of ἐκγίγνομαι ‘be born of’, with the parent in the genitive. Ἶλός τε Ἀσσάρακός τε καὶ … Γανυμήδης names the three. ἀμύμονες ‘blameless’ and ἀντίθεος ‘godlike’ are stock epithets, translated every time. κάλλιστος ‘most beautiful’ is the superlative of καλός, with θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων as in line 220.

sentences.t:
τὸν καὶ ἀνηρείψαντο θεοὶ Διὶ οἰνοχοεύειν
κάλλεος εἵνεκα οἷο ἵν’ ἀθανάτοισι μετείη.
sentences.tr:
ton kai anēreipsanto theoi Dii oinochoeuein
kalleos heineka hoio hin’ athanatoisi meteiē.
sentences.l:
Him even the gods snatched away, to pour wine for Zeus,
on account of his own beauty, that he might be among the immortals.
sentences.i: The gods even carried him off to pour wine for Zeus, for the sake of his beauty, so that he might be among the immortals.
sentences.n: τὸν καί: τόν ‘him’ is Ganymede and καί ‘even’. ἀνηρείψαντο is the aorist middle of ἀνερείπομαι ‘snatch away’. Διὶ οἰνοχοεύειν ‘to pour wine for Zeus’: the infinitive of οἰνοχοεύω gives the purpose. κάλλεος is the epic genitive of κάλλος ‘beauty’; εἵνεκα ‘on account of’ follows it, and οἷο is the epic reflexive genitive ‘his own’. μετείη ‘might be among’. The Odyssey has the second line for Dawn’s taking of Cleitus.

sentences.t: Ἶλος δ’ αὖ τέκεθ’ υἱὸν ἀμύμονα Λαομέδοντα·
sentences.tr: Ilos d’ au teketh’ huion amymona Laomedonta·
sentences.l: and Ilus in turn begot a son, blameless Laomedon;
sentences.i: Ilus in turn begot a blameless son, Laomedon;
sentences.n: Ἶλος is the subject and τέκεθ’ is τέκετο elided. Λαομέδοντα is the accusative of Λαομέδων, in apposition to υἱὸν ἀμύμονα ‘a blameless son’; the next line makes him the father of Priam. ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ is the stock epithet again.

sentences.t:
Λαομέδων δ’ ἄρα Τιθωνὸν τέκετο Πρίαμόν τε
Λάμπόν τε Κλυτίον θ’ Ἱκετάονά τ’ ὄζον Ἄρηος·
sentences.tr:
Laomedōn d’ ara Tithōnon teketo Priamon te
Lampon te Klytion th’ Hiketaona t’ ozon Arēos·
sentences.l:
and Laomedon then begot Tithonus and Priam
and Lampus and Clytius and Hicetaon, scion of Ares;
sentences.i: and Laomedon then begot Tithonus and Priam, Lampus and Clytius and Hicetaon, scion of Ares;
sentences.n: Λαομέδων is the subject; the five sons are in the accusative, the last four each with τε ‘and’: Τιθωνόν, Πρίαμον, Λάμπον, Κλυτίον, Ἱκετάονα. ὄζον Ἄρηος ‘scion of Ares’ (ὄζος is a branch or shoot) is the same stock phrase for Hicetaon as in the line about the elders at 3.147. Ἄρηος is the epic genitive of Ἄρης. Priam is thus reached through Ilus’ line.

sentences.t: Ἀσσάρακος δὲ Κάπυν, ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ Ἀγχίσην τέκε παῖδα·
sentences.tr: Assarakos de Kapyn, ho d’ ar’ Anchisēn teke paida·
sentences.l: and Assaracus Capys, and he then begot Anchises as a son;
sentences.i: Assaracus begot Capys, and Capys begot a son, Anchises;
sentences.n: Ἀσσάρακος δὲ Κάπυν: the verb τέκετο is not repeated but understood from the lines before, so Assaracus is the subject and Κάπυν the object. ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ‘and he then’ takes up Capys as the subject of τέκε ‘begot’, with Ἀγχίσην … παῖδα ‘Anchises as a son’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔμ’ Ἀγχίσης, Πρίαμος δ’ ἔτεχ’ Ἕκτορα δῖον.
ταύτης τοι γενεῆς τε καὶ αἵματος εὔχομαι εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
autar em’ Anchisēs, Priamos d’ etech’ Hektora dion.
tautēs toi geneēs te kai haimatos euchomai einai.
sentences.l:
but me Anchises, and Priam begot heavenly Hector.
Of this lineage, I tell you, and of this blood I claim to be.
sentences.i: Anchises begot me, and Priam begot heavenly Hector. I tell you, I claim to be of this lineage and this blood.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔμ’ Ἀγχίσης: ἔμ’ is the elided accusative ἐμέ, and the one verb ἔτεχ’ (ἔτεκε ‘begot’) serves both Ἀγχίσης and Πρίαμος, whose lines have now been traced down to Aeneas and to Hector (δῖον ‘heavenly’, the stock epithet). ταύτης … γενεῆς τε καὶ αἵματος εὔχομαι εἶναι ‘I claim to be of this lineage and blood’; τοι is ‘I tell you’. Glaucus ends his genealogy with the same line at 6.211; here Aeneas’ speech goes on.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δ’ ἀρετὴν ἄνδρεσσιν ὀφέλλει τε μινύθει τε
ὅππως κεν ἐθέλῃσιν·
sentences.tr:
Zeus d’ aretēn andressin ophellei te minythei te
hoppōs ken ethelēisin·
sentences.l:
And Zeus excellence for men both increases and lessens
in whatever way he may wish;
sentences.i: Zeus both increases and lessens the excellence of men, in whatever way he wishes;
sentences.n: ὀφέλλει ‘increases’ and μινύθει ‘lessens’ are opposite verbs with the same object ἀρετήν ‘excellence’ (what makes a man succeed in battle) and Zeus as subject, joined by τε … τε. ἄνδρεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ἀνήρ. ὅππως κεν ἐθέλῃσιν ‘in whatever way he wishes’ has κεν and the subjunctive of ἐθέλω, a general clause; ὅππως is an epic form of ὅπως.

sentences.t: ὃ γὰρ κάρτιστος ἁπάντων.
sentences.tr: ho gar kartistos hapantōn.
sentences.l: for he is the strongest of all.
sentences.i: for he is the strongest of all.
sentences.n: ὃ is the demonstrative ‘he’ (Zeus), a pronoun here, not the neuter relative. κάρτιστος ‘strongest’ is the superlative related to κράτος ‘strength’, with the genitive ἁπάντων ‘of all’. This is the reason Zeus is free to raise a man’s excellence or lower it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μηκέτι ταῦτα λεγώμεθα νηπύτιοι ὣς
ἑσταότ’ ἐν μέσσῃ ὑσμίνῃ δηϊοτῆτος.
sentences.tr:
all’ age mēketi tauta legōmetha nēpytioi hōs
hestaot’ en messēi hysminēi dēïotētos.
sentences.l:
But come, let us no longer talk these things over, like babes,
standing in the middle of the battle’s fighting.
sentences.i: But come, let us no longer stand here talking these things over like children in the middle of the battle’s fighting.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μηκέτι … λεγώμεθα is an exhortation, the subjunctive of λέγομαι, here ‘talk over’; ταῦτα ‘these things’. νηπύτιοι ὣς ‘like babes’ and ἑσταότ’ (ἑσταότες, elided, the perfect participle of ἵστημι ‘standing’) agree with the subject ‘we’. ἐν μέσσῃ ὑσμίνῃ δηϊοτῆτος ‘in the middle of the battle of fighting’, with the epic doubled σ in μέσσῃ. Line 244 stands also at 13.292.

sentences.t:
ἔστι γὰρ ἀμφοτέροισιν ὀνείδεα μυθήσασθαι
πολλὰ μάλ’, οὐδ’ ἂν νηῦς ἑκατόζυγος ἄχθος ἄροιτο.
sentences.tr:
esti gar amphoteroisin oneidea mythēsasthai
polla mal’, oud’ an nēus hekatozygos achthos aroito.
sentences.l:
For there are for both of us reproaches to speak,
very many, and not a hundred-benched ship could bear the load.
sentences.i: For there are very many reproaches that both of us could speak, and not even a hundred-benched ship could carry the load.
sentences.n: ἔστι with an infinitive means ‘it is possible’: ὀνείδεα ‘reproaches’ (epic plural) are things both men (ἀμφοτέροισιν, dative) can speak. πολλὰ μάλ’ ‘very many’. οὐδ’ ἂν … ἄροιτο ‘not even … could bear’ is a potential optative, the aorist middle of αἴρω ‘take up’. νηῦς ἑκατόζυγος is a ship of a hundred benches, ζυγά being the rowers’ benches. ἄχθος ‘burden, load’.

sentences.t:
στρεπτὴ δὲ γλῶσσ’ ἐστὶ βροτῶν, πολέες δ’ ἔνι μῦθοι
παντοῖοι, ἐπέων δὲ πολὺς νομὸς ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.
sentences.tr:
streptē de glōss’ esti brotōn, polees d’ eni mythoi
pantoioi, epeōn de polys nomos entha kai entha.
sentences.l:
And turnable is the tongue of mortals, and many in it are tales
of every kind, and of words wide is the pasture this way and that.
sentences.i: The tongue of mortals can be turned any way, and there are many tales in it of every kind, and a wide pasture of words this way and that.
sentences.n: A saying about speech. στρεπτή ‘turnable’ comes from τρέπω ‘turn’: the tongue can be turned to anything. βροτῶν ‘of mortals’. ἔνι is ἔνεστι ‘are in it’. πολέες is the epic form of πολλοί, παντοῖοι ‘of every kind’, and ἐπέων the epic genitive plural of ἔπος. νομός ‘pasture, range’ is the grazing ground for words, ‘this way and that’ being ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.

sentences.t: ὁπποῖόν κ’ εἴπῃσθα ἔπος, τοῖόν κ’ ἐπακούσαις.
sentences.tr: hoppoion k’ eipēistha epos, toion k’ epakousais.
sentences.l: Whatever sort of word you may speak, such a one you might hear in return.
sentences.i: Whatever kind of word you say, you may hear one of the same kind in return.
sentences.n: A proverb in two halves: ὁπποῖον (= ὁποῖον) ‘of whatever sort’ is matched by τοῖον ‘of that sort’. κ’ is κεν in both halves. εἴπῃσθα is the aorist subjunctive of εἶπον with the epic ending -σθα for the second person; ἐπακούσαις is the aorist optative of ἐπακούω ‘hear’, ‘you might hear back’. The saying is turned on Achilles: his taunts will be returned.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τί ἢ ἔριδας καὶ νείκεα νῶϊν ἀνάγκη
νεικεῖν ἀλλήλοισιν ἐναντίον ὥς τε γυναῖκας,
sentences.tr:
alla ti ē eridas kai neikea nōïn anankē
neikein allēloisin enantion hōs te gynaikas,
sentences.l:
But why indeed is it necessary for us two strifes and quarrels
to rebuke, each other, face to face, like women,
sentences.i: But why must the two of us carry on strifes and quarrels, rebuking each other face to face like women,
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ τί ἢ opens a rhetorical question, ‘but why then…?’. ἀνάγκη ‘(it is) necessary’ has ἐστί left out and takes the infinitive νεικεῖν ‘to rebuke’; ἔριδας καὶ νείκεα ‘strifes and quarrels’ are its object, from the same root as the verb. νῶϊν is the dual dative ‘for us two’. ἐναντίον ‘opposite, face to face’; ὥς τε γυναῖκας ‘just like women’. The unit stops at a comma because the comparison continues for three more lines.

sentences.t:
αἵ τε χολωσάμεναι ἔριδος πέρι θυμοβόροιο
νεικεῦσ’ ἀλλήλῃσι μέσην ἐς ἄγυιαν ἰοῦσαι
πόλλ’ ἐτεά τε καὶ οὐκί· χόλος δέ τε καὶ τὰ κελεύει.
sentences.tr:
hai te cholōsamenai eridos peri thymoboroio
neikeus’ allēlēisi mesēn es aguian iousai
poll’ etea te kai ouki· cholos de te kai ta keleuei.
sentences.l:
who, having been angered, over heart-devouring strife
rebuke one another, going into the middle of the street,
many things both true and not; and anger bids these things too.
sentences.i: who, angered over heart-devouring strife, go out into the middle of the street and rebuke each other, saying many things both true and untrue; anger prompts these too.
sentences.n: αἵ τε ‘who’ opens a general description of what women do. χολωσάμεναι is the aorist participle of χολόω ‘be angered’ (χόλος ‘anger’); ἔριδος πέρι ‘over strife’ has the preposition after its noun; θυμοβόροιο ‘heart-devouring’. νεικεῦσ’ is νεικεῦσι, the third plural of νεικέω ‘rebuke’, with ἰοῦσαι ‘going’. ἄγυιαν ‘street’. ἐτεά ‘true things’ is set against οὐκί ‘not’. χόλος ‘anger’ is the subject of κελεύει.

sentences.t:
ἀλκῆς δ’ οὔ μ’ ἐπέεσσιν ἀποτρέψεις μεμαῶτα
πρὶν χαλκῷ μαχέσασθαι ἐναντίον·
sentences.tr:
alkēs d’ ou m’ epeessin apotrepseis memaōta
prin chalkōi machesasthai enantion·
sentences.l:
From might not with words will you turn me, eager
before with bronze I fight face to face;
sentences.i: You will not turn me from my might with words, eager as I am, before I have fought you face to face with bronze;
sentences.n: ἀποτρέψεις is the future of ἀποτρέπω ‘turn away from’, with the genitive ἀλκῆς ‘from might’. οὔ μ’ … μεμαῶτα ‘not me, eager’: μεμαῶτα is the perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, agreeing with με. ἐπέεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ἔπος ‘word’. πρὶν χαλκῷ μαχέσασθαι ἐναντίον is πρίν with the infinitive, ‘before fighting face to face with bronze’, bronze standing for the weapon. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε θᾶσσον
γευσόμεθ’ ἀλλήλων χαλκήρεσιν ἐγχείῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
all’ age thasson
geusometh’ allēlōn chalkēresin encheiēisin.
sentences.l:
but come, more quickly
let us taste of each other with bronze-fitted spears.”
sentences.i: but come, let us quickly taste each other with our bronze-fitted spears.”
sentences.n: θᾶσσον is the comparative of ταχύς ‘quick’, used here as an urging ‘quickly’. γευσόμεθ’ is the subjunctive of exhortation of γεύομαι ‘taste’, which takes the genitive ἀλλήλων ‘of each other’. χαλκήρεσιν ‘bronze-fitted’ is the dative plural of χαλκήρης, and ἐγχείῃσιν the epic dative plural of ἐγχείη ‘spear’. Aeneas’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ ἐν δεινῷ σάκει ἤλασεν ὄβριμον ἔγχος
σμερδαλέῳ·
sentences.tr:
ē rha kai en deinōi sakei ēlasen obrimon enchos
smerdaleōi·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and into the dread shield drove his mighty spear,
the frightful one;
sentences.i: So he said, and drove his mighty spear into the dread, frightful shield;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα καί ‘he spoke, and’ ends a speech and begins the action: ἦ is the old ‘he said’, ῥα (= ἄρα) a particle. ἤλασεν ‘drove’ is the aorist of ἐλαύνω; ὄβριμον ἔγχος ‘mighty spear’. ἐν δεινῷ σάκει ‘into the dread shield’, and σμερδαλέῳ ‘frightful’, the first word of line 260, agrees with σάκει. The shield is Achilles’. The paragraph break marks the return to narration.

sentences.t: μέγα δ’ ἀμφὶ σάκος μύκε δουρὸς ἀκωκῇ.
sentences.tr: mega d’ amphi sakos myke douros akōkēi.
sentences.l: and loudly the shield bellowed around the spear’s tip.
sentences.i: and the shield bellowed loudly around the spear’s tip.
sentences.n: μέγα is an adverb, ‘loudly’. μύκε is the aorist of μυκάομαι, a verb for the lowing of cattle; the shield is its subject. ἀμφί ‘around’ can be read with the dative δουρὸς ἀκωκῇ ‘the spear’s tip’ (ἀκωκή ‘point, tip’), as the English does, or as a bare adverb with the dative as the cause, ‘at the spear’s point’.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δὲ σάκος μὲν ἀπὸ ἕο χειρὶ παχείῃ
ἔσχετο ταρβήσας·
sentences.tr:
Pēleïdēs de sakos men apo heo cheiri pacheiēi
escheto tarbēsas·
sentences.l:
And Peleus’-son the shield away from himself with a stout hand
held out, having taken fright;
sentences.i: Afraid, the son of Peleus held the shield out away from himself with his stout hand;
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης ‘son of Peleus’ is Achilles. ἀπὸ ἕο … ἔσχετο: ἕο is the epic genitive of the reflexive ‘himself’, and ἔσχετο is the aorist middle of ἔχω, ‘held’, so ‘held the shield away from himself’. χειρὶ παχείῃ ‘with a stout hand’ (παχύς ‘stout’, epic feminine dative -είῃ). ταρβήσας is the aorist participle of ταρβέω ‘be afraid’; the γάρ clause that follows says why.

sentences.t:
φάτο γὰρ δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος
ῥέα διελεύσεσθαι μεγαλήτορος Αἰνείαο
νήπιος,
sentences.tr:
phato gar dolichoskion enchos
rhea dieleusesthai megalētoros Aineiao
nēpios,
sentences.l:
for he thought the long-shadowed spear
would easily go through, that of great-spirited Aeneas,
foolish,
sentences.i: for he thought that the long-shadowed spear of great-spirited Aeneas would pass through with ease, foolish as he was,
sentences.n: φάτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of φημί, ‘he said’ in the sense ‘he supposed’. δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος ‘long-shadowed spear’ is a stock phrase. διελεύσεσθαι is the future infinitive of διέρχομαι ‘go through’, and ῥέα ‘easily’. μεγαλήτορος Αἰνείαο ‘of great-spirited Aeneas’ is the owner of the spear. νήπιος ‘foolish’ is the poet’s comment on Achilles. The unit stops at its comma because the sentence runs five lines.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἐνόησε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμὸν
ὡς οὐ ῥηΐδι’ ἐστὶ θεῶν ἐρικυδέα δῶρα
ἀνδράσι γε θνητοῖσι δαμήμεναι οὐδ’ ὑποείκειν.
sentences.tr:
oud’ enoēse kata phrena kai kata thymon
hōs ou rhēïdi’ esti theōn erikydea dōra
andrasi ge thnētoisi damēmenai oud’ hypoeikein.
sentences.l:
and he did not perceive, in mind and in heart,
that not easy are the glorious gifts of the gods
for mortal men to be mastered, nor to give way.
sentences.i: and did not realise, in his mind and heart, that the glorious gifts of the gods are not easily mastered by mortal men, nor made to give way.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἐνόησε ‘and he did not perceive’, with κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν ‘in mind and in heart’. ὡς is ‘that’. ῥηΐδι’ is ῥηΐδια ‘easy’ (Attic ῥᾴδια), neuter plural; ἐρικυδέα ‘glorious’. δαμήμεναι, the aorist passive infinitive of δάμνημι, is ‘be mastered’, and ὑποείκειν is ‘give way’ (ὑπείκειν); both go with ἀνδράσι θνητοῖσι ‘for mortal men’. The gifts of the gods are the armour made by Hephaestus, as the next lines show.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ τότ’ Αἰνείαο δαΐφρονος ὄβριμον ἔγχος
ῥῆξε σάκος·
sentences.tr:
oude tot’ Aineiao daïphronos obrimon enchos
rhēxe sakos·
sentences.l:
Nor then did the mighty spear of wise-minded Aeneas
break the shield;
sentences.i: Nor then did the mighty spear of wise-hearted Aeneas break the shield;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ τότ’ ‘nor then’. ῥῆξε is the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’; its subject is ὄβριμον ἔγχος ‘mighty spear’, and σάκος is the object. δαΐφρονος ‘wise-hearted’ is a stock epithet whose sense is disputed: ‘wise-minded’ (from the root of δαῆναι ‘learn’) or ‘fierce’ (from δαΐ ‘in battle’). ‘Wise-minded’ in the literal English and ‘wise-hearted’ in the free English are followed each time.

sentences.t: χρυσὸς γὰρ ἐρύκακε, δῶρα θεοῖο·
sentences.tr: chrysos gar erykake, dōra theoio·
sentences.l: for gold held it back, gifts of the god;
sentences.i: for the gold held it back, the gifts of the god;
sentences.n: χρυσός ‘gold’ gives the reason. ἐρύκακε is the reduplicated aorist of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’. δῶρα θεοῖο ‘gifts of the god’ is in apposition to the gold; θεοῖο is the epic genitive, and the god, Hephaestus, is named by an epithet in line 270.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ δύω μὲν ἔλασσε διὰ πτύχας, αἳ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔτι τρεῖς
ἦσαν, ἐπεὶ πέντε πτύχας ἤλασε κυλλοποδίων,
τὰς δύο χαλκείας, δύο δ’ ἔνδοθι κασσιτέροιο,
τὴν δὲ μίαν χρυσῆν, τῇ ῥ’ ἔσχετο μείλινον ἔγχος.
sentences.tr:
alla dyō men elasse dia ptychas, hai d’ ar’ eti treis
ēsan, epei pente ptychas ēlase kyllopodiōn,
tas dyo chalkeias, dyo d’ endothi kassiteroio,
tēn de mian chrysēn, tēi rh’ escheto meilinon enchos.
sentences.l:
But two it drove through the folds, and they then still three
were, since five folds he had beaten out, the crook-footed one,
the two of bronze, and two inside of tin,
and the one of gold, in which the ashen spear was held fast.
sentences.i: It drove through two of the layers, but three were still left, since the crook-footed god had beaten out five layers: the two of bronze, two inside of tin, and the one of gold, where the ashen spear was held fast.
sentences.n: δύω (= δύο) ‘two’ goes with πτύχας ‘folds’, the sheets of metal laid one over another; ἔλασσε ‘drove’ is the aorist of ἐλαύνω, which is also the metalworker’s verb for beating metal, as in ἤλασε ‘beat out’. κυλλοποδίων ‘the crook-footed one’ is Hephaestus (κυλλός ‘crooked’, πούς ‘foot’), translated every time. κασσιτέροιο is the genitive of κασσίτερος ‘tin’. μείλινον ‘ashen’ comes from μελίη ‘ash’. ἔσχετο ‘was held fast’. Two and two and one make the five folds.

sentences.t:
δεύτερος αὖτ’ Ἀχιλεὺς προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος,
καὶ βάλεν Αἰνείαο κατ’ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην
ἄντυγ’ ὕπο πρώτην, ᾗ λεπτότατος θέε χαλκός,
λεπτοτάτη δ’ ἐπέην ῥινὸς βοός·
sentences.tr:
deuteros aut’ Achileus proïei dolichoskion enchos,
kai balen Aineiao kat’ aspida pantos’ eïsēn
antyg’ hypo prōtēn, hēi leptotatos thee chalkos,
leptotatē d’ epeēn rhinos boos·
sentences.l:
Second in turn Achilles sent forth his long-shadowed spear,
and struck, on the shield of Aeneas, equal on every side,
under the outermost rim, where thinnest ran the bronze,
and thinnest lay upon it of ox-hide;
sentences.i: Achilles in his turn, throwing second, sent forth his long-shadowed spear, and struck Aeneas on his shield, equal on every side, under the outermost rim, where the bronze ran thinnest and the thinnest layer of ox-hide lay upon it;
sentences.n: δεύτερος αὖτ’ ‘second in turn’; προΐει ‘sent forth’ is the imperfect of προΐημι. βάλεν Αἰνείαο κατ’ ἀσπίδα ‘struck on the shield of Aeneas’: Αἰνείαο is the genitive of possession with ἀσπίδα, and κατά with the accusative is ‘on’. πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην ‘equal on every side’ means perfectly round. ἄντυξ is the rim of the shield, and πρώτην here is ‘outermost’. ᾗ is ‘where’, θέε ‘ran’. ἐπέην is the epic ἐπῆν ‘was upon’, with ῥινὸς βοός ‘of ox-hide’ giving the material.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ διὰ πρὸ
Πηλιὰς ἤϊξεν μελίη, λάκε δ’ ἀσπὶς ὑπ’ αὐτῆς.
sentences.tr:
hē de dia pro
Pēlias ēïxen meliē, lake d’ aspis hyp’ autēs.
sentences.l:
and it, right through,
the Pelian ash-spear rushed, and the shield cracked under it.
sentences.i: and the Pelian ash-spear rushed right through, and the shield cracked under it.
sentences.n: ἣ δέ ‘and it’ is the spear, feminine like μελίη ‘ash-spear’; Πηλιάς ‘Pelian’ means made of wood from Mount Pelion. διὰ πρό is ‘right through’. ἤϊξεν is the aorist of ἀΐσσω ‘dart, rush’. λάκε is the aorist of λάσκω, a verb of sharp sound; whether the shield cracked or rang is not settled, and ‘cracked’ is used, as at 13.616. ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ‘under it’, the spear’s blow.

sentences.t:
Αἰνείας δ’ ἐάλη καὶ ἀπὸ ἕθεν ἀσπίδ’ ἀνέσχε
δείσας·
sentences.tr:
Aineias d’ ealē kai apo hethen aspid’ anesche
deisas·
sentences.l:
And Aeneas crouched, and away from himself held up the shield,
afraid;
sentences.i: Aeneas, afraid, crouched down and held the shield up away from himself;
sentences.n: ἐάλη is the aorist passive of εἴλω ‘press together’, here ‘crouched’. ἀπὸ ἕθεν ‘away from himself’, ἕθεν being the epic reflexive genitive; ἀνέσχε ‘held up’ is the aorist of ἀνέχω. δείσας is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἐγχείη δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ νώτου ἐνὶ γαίῃ
ἔστη ἱεμένη, διὰ δ’ ἀμφοτέρους ἕλε κύκλους
ἀσπίδος ἀμφιβρότης·
sentences.tr:
encheiē d’ ar’ hyper nōtou eni gaiēi
estē hiemenē, dia d’ amphoterous hele kyklous
aspidos amphibrotēs·
sentences.i: and the spear, still eager to go on, stood fixed in the ground over his back, after tearing through both circles of the man-covering shield;
sentences.n: ἐγχείη ‘spear’ is Achilles’ spear, now past Aeneas. ὑπὲρ νώτου ‘over his back’; ἐνὶ γαίῃ ‘in the earth’. ἱεμένη is the present participle of ἵεμαι ‘be eager, speed on’: the spear stands as if still wanting to fly. διὰ δ’ … ἕλε is a split compound, ‘tore through’ (aorist of αἱρέω). κύκλους ‘circles’ are the rings of the shield. ἀσπίδος ἀμφιβρότης ‘man-covering shield’ (ἀμφί + βροτός).

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀλευάμενος δόρυ μακρὸν
ἔστη, κὰδ δ’ ἄχος οἱ χύτο μυρίον ὀφθαλμοῖσι,
ταρβήσας ὅ οἱ ἄγχι πάγη βέλος.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ aleuamenos dory makron
estē, kad d’ achos hoi chyto myrion ophthalmoisi,
tarbēsas ho hoi anchi pagē belos.
sentences.l:
and he, having avoided the long spear,
stood, and down grief poured for him, countless, over his eyes,
afraid because near him the shaft was fixed.
sentences.i: He stood still, having avoided the long spear, and countless grief poured down over his eyes, afraid because the shaft had stuck fast so near him.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Aeneas. ἀλευάμενος is the aorist participle of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’. κὰδ δ’ … χύτο is κατά by assimilation before δ, with the aorist middle χύτο of χέω ‘pour’ (unaugmented): ‘grief poured down’. οἱ ‘for him’, ὀφθαλμοῖσι ‘over his eyes’. μυρίον ‘countless’. ὅ here is ‘because’ (= ὅτι), and πάγη is the aorist passive of πήγνυμι ‘fix, stick’. βέλος ‘shaft’ is the spear.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἐμμεμαὼς ἐπόρουσεν ἐρυσσάμενος ξίφος ὀξὺ
σμερδαλέα ἰάχων·
sentences.tr:
autar Achilleus
emmemaōs eporousen eryssamenos xiphos oxy
smerdalea iachōn·
sentences.i: but Achilles, eager, rushed upon him with his sharp sword drawn, crying out terribly;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεύς ‘but Achilles’ sets him against the frightened Aeneas. ἐμμεμαώς ‘eager’ is the perfect participle of ἐμμέμονα. ἐπόρουσεν ‘rushed upon’ is the aorist of ἐπορούω. ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρύω ‘draw’. ξίφος ὀξύ ‘sharp sword’. σμερδαλέα ἰάχων ‘crying out terribly’: σμερδαλέα is a neuter plural used as an adverb, and ἰάχων the participle of ἰάχω.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ χερμάδιον λάβε χειρὶ
Αἰνείας, μέγα ἔργον, ὃ οὐ δύο γ’ ἄνδρε φέροιεν,
οἷοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσ’·
sentences.tr:
ho de chermadion labe cheiri
Aineias, mega ergon, ho ou dyo g’ andre pheroien,
hoioi nyn brotoi eis’·
sentences.i: And Aeneas took in his hand a rock, a great piece of work, one that two men, such as mortals now are, could not carry;
sentences.n: ὃ δὲ … Αἰνείας: the pronoun ‘he’ comes first and the name follows. χερμάδιον ‘rock’ is a stone fit for throwing, and μέγα ἔργον ‘a great work’ is in apposition. ὃ οὐ δύο γ’ ἄνδρε φέροιεν is a potential optative with the dual ἄνδρε ‘two men’. οἷοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσ’ ‘such as mortals now are’ says that men of the poet’s day are weaker than the heroes. The same words are used of Diomedes’ rock at 5.302–304.

sentences.t: ὃ δέ μιν ῥέα πάλλε καὶ οἶος.
sentences.tr: ho de min rhea palle kai oios.
sentences.l: but he easily swung it, and alone.
sentences.i: but he swung it easily, even alone.
sentences.n: μιν is ‘it’, the rock. πάλλε is the imperfect of πάλλω ‘swing, brandish’, and ῥέα ‘easily’. οἶος is ‘alone’ (Attic μόνος), so καὶ οἶος is ‘even alone’. The same half-line follows Diomedes’ rock at 5.304.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κεν Αἰνείας μὲν ἐπεσσύμενον βάλε πέτρῳ
ἢ κόρυθ’ ἠὲ σάκος, τό οἱ ἤρκεσε λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον,
τὸν δέ κε Πηλεΐδης σχεδὸν ἄορι θυμὸν ἀπηύρα,
εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.tr:
entha ken Aineias men epessymenon bale petrōi
ē koryth’ ēe sakos, to hoi ērkese lygron olethron,
ton de ke Pēleïdēs schedon aori thymon apēura,
ei mē ar’ oxy noēse Poseidaōn enosichthōn·
sentences.l:
Then Aeneas would have struck him, as he rushed on, with the rock,
either on helmet or shield, which would have warded off grievous destruction from him,
and him Peleus’-son at close quarters with the sword would have taken the life from,
if not then sharply had noticed Poseidon earth-shaker;
sentences.i: Then Aeneas would have struck him with the rock as he rushed at him, either on his helmet or on his shield, which would have warded off grievous destruction from him, and the son of Peleus would have taken Aeneas’ life from him with his sword at close quarters, had Poseidon earth-shaker not been quick to notice;
sentences.n: ἔνθά κεν … βάλε, with κεν and an aorist, is a past unreal case: Aeneas ‘would have struck’. ἐπεσσύμενον is the participle of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush at’, and the object ‘him’ is Achilles. τό … ἤρκεσε is the relative clause with the same ‘would have’: ἀρκέω ‘ward off’, with λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον ‘grievous destruction’. θυμὸν ἀπηύρα ‘would have taken the life from’ is from ἀπαυράω. εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε is the stock rescue-formula. ἐνοσίχθων ‘earth-shaker’.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖς μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr: autika d’ athanatoisi theois meta mython eeipen·
sentences.l: And at once among the immortal gods a speech he spoke:
sentences.i: At once he spoke among the immortal gods:
sentences.n: αὐτίκα ‘at once’. μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπεν ‘spoke a speech among’ is a formula for speaking to a group: μετά takes the dative ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖς ‘immortal gods’, and ἔειπεν is the aorist with doubled ε. Poseidon speaks to the gods who have come down to watch the fight with him, and the colon opens his speech.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ μοι ἄχος μεγαλήτορος Αἰνείαο,
ὃς τάχα Πηλεΐωνι δαμεὶς Ἄϊδος δὲ κάτεισι
πειθόμενος μύθοισιν Ἀπόλλωνος ἑκάτοιο
νήπιος, οὐδέ τί οἱ χραισμήσει λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi ē moi achos megalētoros Aineiao,
hos tacha Pēleïōni dameis Aïdos de kateisi
peithomenos mythoisin Apollōnos hekatoio
nēpios, oude ti hoi chraismēsei lygron olethron.
sentences.l:
“Ah, truly for me grief for great-spirited Aeneas,
who soon, overcome by Peleus’-son, to Hades will go down,
obeying the words of Apollo, of the far-darter,
foolish, and not at all will he avail him against grievous destruction.
sentences.i: “Ah, truly I grieve for great-spirited Aeneas, who will soon go down to Hades, overcome by the son of Peleus, because he obeyed the words of Apollo the far-darter, foolish as he is; and Apollo will not help him at all against grievous destruction.
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι ‘ah’ is an exclamation of dismay. ἦ μοι ἄχος … Αἰνείαο ‘truly to me (there is) grief for Aeneas’, with ἄχος ‘grief’ and Αἰνείαο an objective genitive. Πηλεΐωνι, a form of the patronymic, is ‘the son of Peleus’; δαμείς is the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι. Ἄϊδος δὲ κάτεισι: Ἄϊδος δέ, printed as two words, is the genitive Ἄϊδος with the ending -δε ‘to’ (‘to the house of Hades’), and κάτεισι is the future of κάτειμι ‘go down’. ἑκάτοιο ‘of the far-darter’ (the sense of ἕκατος alone is not certain). χραισμήσει has Apollo as its subject, from χραισμέω ‘help’.

sentences.l:
But why indeed does this man now, blameless, suffer pains
in vain, for the sake of others’ griefs, and pleasing, always,
gifts to the gods give, who hold the wide heaven?
sentences.i: But why does this blameless man suffer pains now, to no purpose, for the sake of other men’s griefs, when he always gives pleasing gifts to the gods who hold the wide heaven?
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ τί ἢ νῦν ‘but why now?’ opens a question to the other gods. οὗτος ‘this man’ is Aeneas. ἀναίτιος ‘blameless’ is ἀ- ‘not’ with αἴτιος ‘to blame’. ἄλγεα πάσχει ‘suffers pains’. μὰψ ‘in vain’; ἕνεκ’ ἀλλοτρίων ἀχέων ‘for the sake of others’ griefs’, that is, troubles that are not his own. κεχαρισμένα ‘pleasing’ is the perfect passive participle of χαρίζομαι. τοί is the old relative ‘who’ (= οἵ).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ἡμεῖς πέρ μιν ὑπὲκ θανάτου ἀγάγωμεν,
μή πως καὶ Κρονίδης κεχολώσεται, αἴ κεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
τόνδε κατακτείνῃ·
sentences.tr:
all’ ageth’ hēmeis per min hypek thanatou agagōmen,
mē pōs kai Kronidēs kecholōsetai, ai ken Achilleus
tonde katakteinēi·
sentences.i: But come, let us ourselves bring him out from under death, lest the son of Cronus be angered too, if Achilles should kill this man;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ is ἀλλ’ ἄγετε ‘but come’ (the θ is the aspirate carried back from the rough breathing of ἡμεῖς). ἡμεῖς πέρ ‘we ourselves’. ὑπὲκ θανάτου ‘out from under death’ is ὑπό + ἐκ; ἀγάγωμεν is the aorist subjunctive of ἄγω, an exhortation. μή πως … κεχολώσεται ‘lest … be angered’ has the future perfect of χολόω. Κρονίδης ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus. αἴ κεν … κατακτείνῃ ‘if he should kill’, with τόνδε ‘this man here’.

sentences.t:
μόριμον δέ οἵ ἐστ’ ἀλέασθαι,
ὄφρα μὴ ἄσπερμος γενεὴ καὶ ἄφαντος ὄληται
Δαρδάνου, ὃν Κρονίδης περὶ πάντων φίλατο παίδων
οἳ ἕθεν ἐξεγένοντο γυναικῶν τε θνητάων.
sentences.tr:
morimon de hoi est’ aleasthai,
ophra mē aspermos geneē kai aphantos olētai
Dardanou, hon Kronidēs peri pantōn philato paidōn
hoi hethen exegenonto gynaikōn te thnētaōn.
sentences.l:
for it is fated for him to escape,
so that not seedless and unseen may the lineage perish
of Dardanus, whom the son-of-Cronus loved above all the sons
who were born of him, and of mortal women.
sentences.i: for it is fated for him to escape, so that the lineage of Dardanus may not perish seedless and unseen, Dardanus whom the son of Cronus loved above all the sons born to him of mortal women.
sentences.n: μόριμον ‘fated’ (from μόρος ‘lot’) with the dative οἵ ‘for him’ and the infinitive ἀλέασθαι ‘to escape’, the aorist of ἀλέομαι. ὄφρα μὴ … ὄληται is a purpose clause, with the aorist subjunctive of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’; ἄσπερμος ‘seedless’ and ἄφαντος ‘unseen’ are predicates of γενεή ‘lineage’. Δαρδάνου depends on γενεή. φίλατο is the aorist middle of φιλέω ‘love’; περὶ πάντων ‘above all’. ἕθεν ‘from him’ is Zeus, so the sons are those he fathered on mortal women (θνητάων, the epic genitive plural).

sentences.t: ἤδη γὰρ Πριάμου γενεὴν ἔχθηρε Κρονίων·
sentences.tr: ēdē gar Priamou geneēn echthēre Kroniōn·
sentences.l: For already Priam’s lineage has the son-of-Cronus come to hate;
sentences.i: For the son of Cronus has already come to hate the lineage of Priam;
sentences.n: ἤδη γάρ ‘for already’. ἔχθηρε is the aorist of ἐχθαίρω, ‘came to hate’. Πριάμου γενεήν ‘the lineage of Priam’: Priam’s branch comes from Ilus, Aeneas’ from Assaracus, as Aeneas himself laid out at 236–240. Κρονίων is a patronymic form for Zeus, ‘the son of Cronus’. The sentence stops at the ano teleia, and the next gives the consequence.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ δὴ Αἰνείαο βίη Τρώεσσιν ἀνάξει
καὶ παίδων παῖδες, τοί κεν μετόπισθε γένωνται.
sentences.tr:
nyn de dē Aineiao biē Trōessin anaxei
kai paidōn paides, toi ken metopisthe genōntai.
sentences.l:
but now indeed the might of Aeneas will be lord over the Trojans,
and his children’s children, who may be born hereafter.”
sentences.i: but now the might of Aeneas will rule the Trojans, and his children’s children, who may be born hereafter.”
sentences.n: νῦν δὲ δή ‘but now indeed’. Αἰνείαο βίη ‘the might of Aeneas’ is a periphrasis: the man is named through his strength. Τρώεσσιν ἀνάξει is the future of ἀνάσσω ‘be lord over’, with the dative. παίδων παῖδες ‘children’s children’ means all descendants. τοί κεν … γένωνται: τοί is ‘who’ (= οἵ), with κεν and the aorist subjunctive ‘may be born’; μετόπισθε ‘afterwards’. Poseidon’s speech, and this part, end here.
